meta.subtitle: Q2 net revenues +21% to $7.1B, client assets $13.08T, ROTCE 44%; BUY with rate and cash-sorting caveats.

advisories: author's published label BUY differs from the composed STRONG BUY

analystSentiment.commentary: We rate Schwab BUY with a $115-$145 target range. The second-quarter 10-Q for the period ended June 30, 2026 shows a broker-dealer and bank hybrid compounding on every client metric: total client assets reached $13.08 trillion at June 30, up 22% year-over-year, and core net new assets were $119.8 billion in the quarter, up 49%. Total net revenues rose 21% to $7.1 billion, while total expenses excluding interest rose only 12% to $3,403 million, lifting the GAAP pre-tax profit margin to 51.9% from 47.9% a year earlier. Diluted EPS was $1.54, up 43%, and return on tangible common equity reached 44% annualized. The top line is net revenues -- net interest revenue, asset-management and administration fees, and trading revenue -- so we anchor on pre-tax margin, ROTCE and capital rather than a gross-margin, EBITDA or free-cash-flow frame, which is not meaningful for a bank and broker balance sheet. At $100.21 the stock trades at 18.3x trailing earnings and about 12.8x the FY27E EPS of $7.83, undemanding for a franchise growing earnings above 30%. Our probability-weighted fair value sits near $120.55, an expected upside of roughly 20% with reward/risk near 1.3x; the derived signal is stronger, but we hold one notch back to BUY because net interest revenue and bank deposit account fees are rate-sensitive and client cash allocation can shift quickly, as it did in 2022-2023. Consensus is Buy, at 18 buy, 3 hold and 1 sell, with a $125.45 target.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: The Charles Schwab Corporation (SCHW), founded in 1971 and headquartered in Westlake, Texas, is a savings and loan holding company providing wealth management, securities brokerage, banking, asset management, custody, and financial advisory services. It serves clients through two segments, Investor Services -- retail brokerage, advisory, banking and trust, and retirement and business services -- and Advisor Services -- custody, trading, banking and trust, and support for independent registered investment advisors. At June 30, 2026 Schwab held $13.08 trillion in client assets across 39.8 million active brokerage accounts and 48.0 million total client accounts, with $6,671.7 billion receiving ongoing advisory services. The revenue model is diversified: in the second quarter net interest revenue was $3,357 million, asset-management and administration fees were $1,825 million, trading revenue was $1,215 million, and bank deposit account fees were $333 million. Principal subsidiaries include the broker-dealer Charles Schwab & Co., the bank Charles Schwab Bank, SSB, and the asset manager Charles Schwab Investment Management. Management estimates U.S. investable wealth exceeds $90 trillion, framing that client-asset base as a fraction of the addressable pool.

thesis.label: BUY
thesis.body: Schwab converts scale into a self-reinforcing asset-gathering engine. The quarter's core net new assets, detailed under Growth, again ran at a mid-single-digit annualized organic pace, and rising client assets feed several revenue engines at once -- net interest revenue, asset-management and administration fees, and trading -- each of which grew double digits, as the financials set out. Because expenses grew far slower than revenue, the GAAP pre-tax margin reached 51.9% and returns on tangible equity stayed high. The result is above-30% EPS growth from a franchise trading at about 12.8x FY27E earnings. The bear case rests on the same rate lever that powers the bull: lower interest rates and client cash sorting would compress net interest revenue and bank deposit account fees.

catalysts: Asset gathering keeps compounding: net new client assets of $118.7 billion in the quarter, with core net new assets of $259.8 billion over the six months, sustain the base that drives every revenue line.
Net interest margin recovery on average interest-earning assets of $445.0 billion, with further room as higher-cost funding rolls off, supports net interest revenue.
Trading and engagement: daily average trades up 57% year-over-year and margin loan balances of $165.1 billion feed trading revenue and net interest revenue.
Capital return: $1.0 billion of buybacks (11.2 million shares) in the quarter plus a common dividend raised to $.32 per share, with consolidated Tier 1 leverage at 8.7%.
New offerings: the launch of Schwab Crypto for Bitcoin and Ethereum, the Portfolio Insights AI tool, and the Forge Global private-market integration widen the product set.
risks: Rate sensitivity: a decline in interest rates would pressure net interest revenue and bank deposit account fees, the rate-sensitive core of the revenue mix.
Client cash sorting: a shift out of sweep cash into higher-yielding alternatives, as in 2022-2023, would raise funding costs; client cash was 9.0% of client assets, down from 9.9%.
Equity-market drawdown: falling markets would reduce asset-based fees, margin lending and trading activity at the same time.
IDA constraints: the 2023 IDA agreement with the TD Depository Institutions limits flexibility on deposit balances and the related fee revenue.
Valuation: at 18.3x trailing earnings the stock already discounts continued growth, leaving limited cushion if metrics slow.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Second-quarter total net revenues were $7,072 million, up 21% year-over-year, and first-half net revenues were $13,554 million, up 18%. Growth was broad: net interest revenue rose 19% to $3,357 million, asset-management and administration fees rose 16% to $1,825 million, trading revenue rose 28% to $1,215 million, and bank deposit account fees rose 35% to $333 million. Total expenses excluding interest rose only 12% to $3,403 million, so income before taxes climbed 31% to $3,669 million and the GAAP pre-tax profit margin reached 51.9%, up from 47.9% a year earlier. Net income was $2,800 million, up 32%, and diluted EPS was $1.54, up 43%; adjusted diluted EPS was $1.62. Return on average common equity was 25% annualized and return on tangible common equity was 44%. The five-year record shows the rate cycle at work: net revenues fell 9.3% in FY23 before recovering to $19.6 billion in FY24 and $23.9 billion in FY25 (up 22%), with FY25 net income of $8.9 billion and diluted EPS of $4.65. Operating leverage is the core of the earnings story, as expense growth ran well below revenue growth and lifted the pre-tax margin. As a broker-dealer and bank hybrid, the income statement carries no gross-margin, operating-income or EBITDA line, so we read pre-tax margin, ROTCE and the revenue mix instead.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: Schwab's balance sheet is a bank's, not an industrial's. Total assets were $517.3 billion at June 30, 2026, up 13% year-over-year, funded largely by bank deposits of $249.7 billion and payables to brokerage clients of $124.0 billion. Stockholders' equity was $50.1 billion. Interest-earning assets averaged $445.0 billion in the quarter, up 5%, and the securities book held available-for-sale securities of $62.5 billion and held-to-maturity securities of $130.6 billion. Bank loans grew 33% year-over-year to $67.0 billion and margin loan balances rose 30% quarter-over-quarter to $165.1 billion, both direct sources of net interest revenue. Client transactional sweep cash ended June at $485.7 billion, up $24.2 billion from the prior quarter on tax seasonality and organic growth. Capital ratios were sound: the consolidated Tier 1 leverage ratio was 8.7% and the adjusted Tier 1 leverage ratio 6.8%. The vendor's FY25 total debt of $1.9 billion and net debt of -$44.1 billion reflect a financial's balance sheet and are not meaningful leverage measures here; long-term debt was $22.7 billion at quarter-end. Equity has been rebuilt from $36.6 billion in FY22 to $49.4 billion in FY25 as the securities portfolio's rate-driven marks eased.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Reported operating cash flow for a bank and broker swings with balance-sheet flows rather than a clean cash-conversion cycle: FY25 operating cash flow was $9.3 billion against $2.7 billion in FY24, and it had run far higher in FY23, so a free-cash-flow or FCF-yield frame is not meaningful here. Capital return is the cleaner signal. In FY25 Schwab repurchased $7.3 billion of stock and paid $2.3 billion of dividends, and in the second quarter it repurchased 11.2 million shares for $1.0 billion while raising the quarterly common dividend to $.32 per share from $.27. It also redeemed $2.1 billion of Series I preferred stock and issued $1.5 billion of Series L preferred stock, and preferred dividends fell to $119 million from $149 million. Capital expenditure has run low -- $548 million in FY25 -- though the second quarter included $792 million of capex, $633 million of it a multi-year software license with an offsetting long-term-debt liability. With capital ratios sound and returns high, the company generates capital well in excess of its modest reinvestment needs, supporting continued buybacks and dividends.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: At $100.21 Schwab trades at 18.3x trailing earnings, about 15.4x next-twelve-month earnings, and roughly 12.8x the FY27E EPS of $7.83. The FY26E EPS of $6.49 implies the same mid-teens forward multiple. For a financial the top line is net revenues, so the vendor's 6.7x price-to-sales carries little meaning and we do not use a gross-margin, EBITDA or free-cash-flow multiple; the EV/EBITDA cell is empty for the same reason. We anchor instead on earnings power and returns: a trailing net margin of 38.8%, ROTCE of 44% annualized, and a pre-tax margin above 50%. Relative to the growth on offer -- net revenues up 21% and EPS up 43% in the quarter, with consensus FY26E revenue of $28.3 billion and FY27E of $31.7 billion -- a low-teens forward multiple is undemanding. The dividend yield is 1.28%. The Street is constructive: 22 analysts rate the stock Buy, at 18 buy, 3 hold and 1 sell, with a consensus target of $125.45 (median $125.50) inside a $91.00-$145.00 range.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Strong asset gathering continues, net interest margin keeps expanding from 3.00% as higher-cost funding rolls off, and operating leverage carries EPS toward the FY27E $7.83; the multiple re-rates and the stock reaches the top of the Street's $145.00 range.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Client assets compound near the current pace, net interest margin holds around current levels, and EPS tracks the FY26E $6.49 and the consensus FY27E estimate; the stock rises toward the consensus $125.45 target on a mid-teens forward multiple.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Interest rates fall and clients sort cash out of sweep balances -- 9.0% of client assets -- into higher-yield alternatives, as in 2022-2023, compressing net interest revenue and bank deposit account fees; an equity drawdown cuts asset-based and trading revenue and the stock retraces toward its 52-week low near $83.96.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight the Base case at 45%, the Bull at 30%, and the Bear at 25%. That yields a probability-weighted fair value near $120.55, an expected upside of about 20% from $100.21, against a bear-case downside near 15% -- reward/risk of roughly 1.3x. On the derived rule those numbers point to a stronger rating, but we hold one notch back to BUY: net interest revenue and bank deposit account fees are the rate-sensitive core of the revenue mix, and the 2022-2023 episode shows how quickly client cash allocation can move against the model. The Bear price near $85.00 sits just below the 52-week low of $83.96 and well below the current price, so it is a real scenario rather than a formality. Our $115-$145 target range brackets the Base implied price and sits inside the Street's $91.00-$145.00 range.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Schwab reports as a single consolidated segment; the vendor breaks out no product or geographic revenue split. Net revenues are diversified across four engines. Net interest revenue was $3,357 million in the second quarter, up 19%, earned on average interest-earning assets of $445.0 billion and funded by bank deposits of $249.7 billion and client sweep cash. Asset-management and administration fees were $1,825 million, up 16%, tied to client assets and $6,671.7 billion of advisory assets. Trading revenue was $1,215 million, up 28%, at revenue per trade of $1.64. Bank deposit account fees were $333 million, up 35%, under the 2023 IDA agreement. The spread of engines lets results hold across environments, but net interest revenue and bank deposit account fees are the rate-sensitive core.

moatFactors.name: Scale
moatFactors.body: Schwab held $13.08 trillion in client assets at June 30, 2026, across 39.8 million active brokerage accounts and 48.0 million total client accounts. Scale spreads fixed technology and compliance costs across a base measured in trillions and keeps expenses excluding interest at 0.11% of average client assets.

moatFactors.name: Switching costs and custody
moatFactors.body: Custody, advisory and banking relationships are sticky: $6,671.7 billion of assets receive ongoing advisory services, and core net new assets were $119.8 billion in the quarter even as off-platform brokered CDs ran off. Moving custodied assets and advisory accounts is costly and disruptive for clients and for independent advisors.

moatFactors.name: Diversified revenue model
moatFactors.body: Four revenue engines -- net interest revenue, asset-management and administration fees, trading, and bank deposit account fees -- let results hold across environments; in the second quarter every line grew double digits while total net revenues rose 21% and the pre-tax margin reached 51.9%.

moatFactors.name: Cost efficiency
moatFactors.body: Expenses excluding interest were 0.11% of average client assets, and second-quarter revenue growth well outpaced expense growth, evidence of durable operating leverage from the low-cost model.

businessMoat.durability: The scale and switching-cost advantages are durable: client assets and advisory balances compound, and the cost of moving custodied assets protects the base. The chief threat to durability is not competitive displacement but the rate cycle: net interest revenue and bank deposit account fees are the rate-sensitive core, and the 2022-2023 cash-sorting episode set out under Risks shows how quickly that core can compress. Pricing power on commissions is limited after the industry moved to zero, leaving asset gathering and net interest management as the levers. On balance the moat is wide but its earnings are cyclical, which is why we rate the equity one notch below the derived signal.

points: Asset gathering is the flywheel: core net new assets of $119.8 billion in the quarter (up 49%) and $259.8 billion over the six months, with June contributing $62.7 billion at a 5.8% annualized organic growth rate.
Client assets reached $13.08 trillion, up 22% year-over-year and 10% from year-end 2025, against an estimated U.S. investable-wealth pool above $90 trillion -- a long runway.
Account growth continues: 1.4 million new brokerage accounts in the quarter (up 26%) brought active brokerage accounts to 39.8 million and total client accounts to 48.0 million.
Lending expands the balance sheet: bank loans up 33% to $67.0 billion and Pledged Asset Line balances up 59% to $33.4 billion feed net interest revenue.
Consensus sees revenue rising from $23.9 billion in FY25 to $28.3 billion in FY26E and $31.7 billion in FY27E, with EPS reaching $7.83.
New products -- Schwab Crypto, the Portfolio Insights AI tool and the Forge Global private-market integration -- extend the platform into digital assets and private markets.

management.leadership: Richard A. Wurster is President and Chief Executive Officer and Michael D. Verdeschi is Managing Director and Chief Financial Officer, titles as of December 31, 2025. Walter W. Bettinger II and Charles R. Schwab serve as Co-Chairmen of the Board, and Jonathan M. Craig is Managing Director and Head of Investor Services. Founder Charles R. Schwab remains a major individual holder. The 2026 proxy reports 2025 results delivered under this team: net revenue of $23.9 billion (up 22%), diluted EPS of $4.65 (up 56%), ROCE of 21% and ROTCE of 38%, with core net new assets of $519.4 billion (up 42%). The second-quarter continuation of that performance -- ROTCE of 44% annualized and a pre-tax margin of 51.9% -- is consistent with the stated Through Clients' Eyes strategy of coupling scale with expense discipline.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation favors buybacks and a growing dividend on top of low reinvestment needs. In FY25 Schwab repurchased $7.3 billion of stock and paid $2.3 billion of dividends; capital expenditure was just $548 million. In the second quarter it repurchased 11.2 million shares for $1.0 billion and raised the quarterly common dividend to $.32 from $.27. It also managed the preferred stack, redeeming $2.1 billion of Series I preferred and issuing $1.5 billion of Series L preferred, which helped cut preferred dividends to $119 million from $149 million. Buybacks reduced the diluted share count to 1,739 million in the quarter from 1,822 million a year earlier. The consolidated Tier 1 leverage ratio of 8.7% and high returns on tangible equity show the franchise generates capital well ahead of its needs, though the 2023 IDA agreement and regulatory capital minimums shape how freely that capital can be deployed.
management.governance: Governance rests on the 2026 proxy statement (DEF 14A, filed April 6, 2026). The board has fourteen directors and will drop to thirteen at the annual meeting, as Ms. Martin-Flickinger is not standing for re-election. Directors serve staggered three-year terms across three classes, a structure that can slow board turnover. The board determined every director independent under NYSE standards except Mr. Schwab, Mr. Bettinger, Mr. Wurster and Ms. Schwab-Pomerantz, so the two Co-Chairman roles sit with non-independent, founder-aligned directors. Related-party dealings are disclosed: some directors and their affiliates have ordinary-course credit transactions with Schwab's banking and brokerage units on arm's-length terms. The most significant related-party event was the February 12, 2025 resale offering in which TD Bank sold 133.8 million voting and 31.7 million non-voting shares for $13.1 billion and Schwab repurchased 19.2 million non-voting shares for $1.5 billion, after which TD Bank ceased to be a 5% holder and the stockholder agreement was terminated.
management.insiderOwnership: Insider and large-holder ownership is disclosed as of March 3, 2026. Founder Charles R. Schwab beneficially owns 103,039,913 shares, or 5.9% of shares outstanding, including shares held through family trusts and partnerships. Directors and executive officers as a group (21 persons) own 110,047,278 shares, or 6.3%. Among outside holders, BlackRock, Inc. reported 96,697,577 shares, or 5.6%. Founder ownership aligns management with shareholders but, combined with the two non-independent Co-Chairman seats and the staggered board, concentrates influence on the founding side.

idiosyncratic: Client cash sorting: bank deposit account fees and net interest revenue depend on client cash balances. In 2022-2023 rapid rate increases drove clients out of sweep cash into higher-yielding alternatives, forcing Schwab onto higher-cost funding and cutting net income. Client cash was 9.0% of client assets at quarter-end, down from 9.9% a year earlier, so the risk remains active.

Interest-rate direction: a decline in rates can compress net interest revenue and bank deposit account fee revenue if asset yields fall faster than funding costs or if mortgage prepayments accelerate; a sharp rise raised funding costs and unrealized securities losses in 2022-2023. Either direction can pressure the rate-sensitive core of the model.

2023 IDA agreement: fees earned on cash swept to the TD Depository Institutions carry minimum and maximum balance commitments that limit Schwab's ability to respond to rate changes and may yield less than deploying the deposits internally.

Securities-portfolio marks: held-to-maturity securities of $130.6 billion and available-for-sale securities of $62.5 billion carry rate-driven unrealized losses that, if they widen, can dent client and market confidence and constrain the ability to attract assets.

Valuation and expectations: at 18.3x trailing earnings and a Street that is 18 buys to 1 sell, the stock discounts continued strong metrics; a slowdown in net new assets or in net interest margin would leave limited support.
risks.systemic: Schwab's results move with the broader economy and markets. General economic, market and geopolitical conditions drive client asset valuations, trading activity and interest rates, all outside the company's control. Federal Reserve monetary policy has a significant effect on net interest revenue, bank deposit account fees and the market value of the investment portfolio; the Fed held the target rate unchanged through the six months ended June 30, 2026 while the 10-year Treasury yield rose 25 basis points to 4.44%. Equity-market declines reduce asset-based fees, margin demand and trading at the same time. As an interconnected financial institution, Schwab is also exposed to contagion: problems at other financial institutions can disrupt markets, raise funding and capital costs, and, even absent direct exposure, harm confidence in the sector. These systemic forces amplify the company's rate and cash-allocation sensitivities.

body: We rate Schwab BUY with a $115-$145 target range, bracketing a Base case near $124. The second-quarter 10-Q shows a diversified broker-dealer and bank hybrid compounding client assets to $13.08 trillion, growing net revenues 21% to $7.1 billion, and converting that into 43% EPS growth through operating leverage at high returns on tangible equity. At about 12.8x FY27E EPS of $7.83 the valuation is undemanding for that growth, and our probability-weighted fair value near $120.55 implies roughly 20% upside with reward/risk near 1.3x.

We hold one notch below the derived signal because the model's rate-sensitive core -- net interest revenue plus bank deposit account fees -- moves with the rate cycle, and the 2022-2023 episode shows client cash can sort away quickly; client cash has already slipped to 9.0% of client assets. The Bear case near $85, just below the 52-week low, is a genuine downside, not a formality.

The catalysts to watch are the pace of core net new assets, still climbing in June, the trajectory of net interest margin from 3.00%, and continued capital return, against the risks of falling rates, cash sorting and an equity drawdown. On balance the reward outweighs the risk at $100.21, and we would add on weakness toward the target-range low.
